newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak opposition to seek referendum on presidency.
newsitem.headline: Slovak opposition to seek referendum on presidency.

text.p: Slovakia's main political opposition parties on Tuesday said they aimed to collect enough signatures needed to hold a referendum calling for the direct election of the country's president.

Ivan Simko, vice-chairman of the Christian-Democratic Movement (KDH) and chair of the petition committee, told a news conference the drive to collect the 350,000 signatures needed would begin on Thursday.
"We want the direct election of the president to reinforce his independent position," Simko said.
The referendum is seen as an attempt to prevent any possibility of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar from assuming presidential powers before the election of a new president.
The current term of President Michal Kovac, elected in March 1993 by parliament, expires in March 1998, six months before Slovakia's next general election scheduled for the following October.

In the present parliament, the ruling coalition and the opposition cannot agree on a common condidate for president and neither can garner the three-fifths majority necessary in the 150-seat house to push through their own choice.
According to the the constitution, Meciar, an avowed political foe of Kovac, would assume presidential powers in the event of an indecisive vote.

"This would have two grave consequences. The interim president could not, for example, sign new laws, which would paralyse the legislature," Jan Budaj, vice-chairman of the opposition Democratic Union (DU) party, told Reuters.
"On the other hand he would have the power...to pardon crimes, and this could be abused to cover up criminal acts and murky privatisation deals."
Simko said the petition committee consisted of the KDH, the DU, the Democratic Party, the Hungarian coalition parties and the Social-Democrats.
If the 350,000 signature minimum were reached, Kovac would be empowered to call a referendum within 90 days. At least 50 percent of the electorate must vote in a referendum to make it valid.
A simple majority of those voting would be needed to pass a resolution that the president be elected directly by the people.
Kovac himself has backed direct election of the head of state, saying this would contribute to his independence and impartiality.
Since 1993 Meciar has made several attempts to oust Kovac, but has failed due to a lack of votes in parliament.
He has, however, managed to whittle down the president's powers, continously slashing the presidential office budget.
Last year Kovac said he would not stand for re-election in 1998 but last week indicated he might change his mind.
